comments.text: 10:36 You are right, there was a study that found that the black plastic utensils contained a flame retardant. However, the study made an error when reporting this finding. They stated that the safe limit for the intake was 42,000 nanograms per day. Their finding was that these utensils could cause an intake of 34,700 nanograms per day. However, the EPA safe limit isn't 42,000 nanograms per day, but 420,000 nanograms. So these things could expose you to less than one tenth of the safe dose. So, while it is still probably better to not use them, the risk isn't nearly as bad as what was originally reported. Thanks for your continued effort to spread good health information and fight the misinformation out there.

comments.text: 10:30 a little fact check on Dr Mike here.  The study that gets cited often for this had a major mathematical error that put the risk from black plastic utensils off by a full magnitude.  So while there are some toxins (mainly flame retardant) from the recycled plastics, they are not remotely as bad as the original study tried to paint them to be.  The exposure you would get from using black plastic utensils with hot food over a day is actually less then a tenth of the EPAs recommended safe dose per day, so really not something you need to be concerned about.  (The author of the paper still kept the same conclusion, but the accurate numbers don't really support their conclusion as much.)
